cues.text: We're very pleased to welcome to our special interest group today, Dr. Linda Graycar who is from the City Institute for the Blind. Linda is going to talk to us about the system of writing for the blind known as Braille. Linda, welcome.
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Thank you.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Now we'd like to keep this session pretty informal, and I know Linda won't mind if members of the group want to ask questions as we go along. Let's start with an obvious one. What is Braille and where does it get its name from?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Well, as you said, Braille is a system of writing used by and for people who cannot see. It gets its name from the man who invented it, the Frenchman Louis Braille who lived in the early 19th century.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Was Louis Braille actually blind himself?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Well ... he wasn't born blind, but he lost his sight at the age of three as the result of an accident in his father's workshop. Louis Braille then went to Paris to the National Institute for Blind Children and that's where he invented his writing system at the age of only 15 in 1824 while he was at the Institute.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: But he wasn't the first person to invent a system of touch reading for the blind, was he?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: No - another Frenchman had already come up with the idea of printing embossed letters that stood out from the paper but this was very cumbersome and inefficient.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Did Louis Braille base his system on this first one?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: No, not really. When he first went to Paris he heard about a military system of writing using twelve dots. This was a system invented by an enterprising French army officer and it was known as ' night writing' It wasn't meant for the blind, but rather ... for battle communications at night.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: That must've been fun!
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Anyway, Braille took this system as a starting point but instead of using the twelve dots which 'night writing' used, he cut the number of dots in half and developed a six-dot system.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Can you give us a little more information about how it works?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Well, it's a system of touch reading which uses an arrangement of raised dots called a cell. Braille numbered the dot positions 1-2-3 downward on the left and 4-5-6 downward on the right. The letters of the alphabet are then formed by using different combinations of these dots.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: So is the writing system based on the alphabet with each word being individually spelt out?
cues.speaker: Student

cues.text: Well ... it's not quite that simple, I'm afraid! For instance, the first 10 letters of the alphabet are formed using dots 1, 2, 4 and 5. But Braille also has its own short forms for common words. For example, 'b' for the word 'but' and 'h' for 'have' - there are many other contractions like this.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: So you spell out most words letter by letter, but you use short forms for common words.
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Yes. Though, I think that makes it sound a little easier than it actually is!
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: And was it immediately accepted? I mean, did it catch on straight away?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Well, yes and no! It was immediately accepted and used by Braille's fellow students at the school but the system was not officially adopted until 1854, two years after Braille's death. So, official acceptance was slow in coming!
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: I suppose it works for all languages which use the roman alphabet?
cues.speaker: Student

cues.text: Yes, it does, with adaptations, of course.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Can it be written by hand or do you need a machine to produce Braille?
cues.speaker: Student

cues.text: Well, you can write it by hand on to paper with a device called a slate and stylus but the trick is that you have to write backwards ... e.g. from right to left so that then when you turn your sheet over, the dots face upwards and can be read like English from left to right.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Oh, I see.
cues.speaker: Student

cues.text: But these days you'd probably use a Braille­writing machine, which is a lot easier!
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: And, tell us, Linda. Is Braille used in other ways? Other than for reading text?
cues.speaker: Chairman

cues.text: Yes, indeed. In addition to the literary Braille code, as it's known, which of course includes English and French, there are other codes. For instance, in 1965 they created a form of Braille for Mathematics.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: I can’t, imagine trying to do maths in Braille!
cues.speaker: Student

cues.text: Yes, that does sound difficult, I agree. And there's also a version for scientific notation. Oh and yes, I almost forgot, there is now a version for music notation as well.
cues.speaker: Dr. Graycar

cues.text: Well, thanks, Linda.
cues.speaker: Chairman
